author: Cyril of Alexandria
occasion: Cyril writes to the emperor to confess the orthodox faith about Christ, affirming one Christ from two natures and rejecting any mixing or confusion of the divine Word with the flesh.
argument: Cyril confesses that the only-begotten Son of God is perfect God, consubstantial with the Father in divinity and consubstantial with us in humanity. He explains that a union of two natures has occurred, so that Christians confess one Christ, one Son, one Lord. He illustrates this with the human composition of soul and body, where two natures form one human being, not two. He warns that if one denies that the one Christ is from two different natures, opponents will ask how the incarnation occurred or what flesh was assumed. Finally, he states that the catholic and apostolic church anathematizes those who say a mixture, confusion, or blending of God the Word with the flesh occurred.

outline.move: Cyril confesses one Christ from two natures, illustrates the union by the soul-body analogy, answers an anticipated objection, and anathematizes those who teach mixture or confusion of the Word with the flesh.

cast.name: Theodosius

voices.how_marked: Introduced by ἐροῦσιν ('they will say'), with οἱ δι' ἐναντίας ('those on the opposite side') marking the opponents

key_terms.sense: Sharing the same being or substance; used of the Son's relation to the Father in divinity and to us in humanity.
The union of two natures, divine and human, in the one Christ.
The composition or putting together of soul and body in a human being, used as an analogy for Christ's two natures.
A mixing or blending of the divine Word with the flesh, which Cyril rejects.
A confusion or merging of the divine Word with the flesh, rejected as heretical.
A mixing together or jumbling of the divine Word with the flesh, rejected as heretical.
The church's formal condemnation or curse upon those who teach mixture or confusion of the Word with the flesh.

_unresolved_facts.claim: He warns that if one denies that the one Christ is from two different natures, opponents will ask how the incarnation occurred or what flesh was assumed.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Ἐὰν γὰρ ἀνέλωμεν τὸ ὅτι ἐκ δύο καὶ διαφόρων φύσεων ὁ εἷς καὶ μόνος ἐστὶ Χριστός, ἐροῦσιν οἱ δι' ἐναντίας· εἰ μία φύσις τὸ ὅλον, πῶς ἐνηνθρώπησεν ἢ ποίαν δὲ ἀνεποιήσατο σάρκα;
_unresolved_facts.fix: Cyril states that if 'we remove/eliminate' (ἀνέλωμεν, subjunctive) the fact that Christ is from two different natures, then opponents will ask their question—not 'if one denies' but 'if we do away with/eliminate' this teaching. The opponents' question assumes a hypothetical where 'one nature is the whole' (εἰ μία φύσις τὸ ὅλον), not simply 'denying' the two-nature position.

_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ἐροῦσιν οἱ δι' ἐναντίας· εἰ μία φύσις τὸ ὅλον, πῶς ἐνηνθρώπησεν ἢ ποίαν δὲ ἀνεποιήσατο σάρκα;
_unresolved_facts.fix: The opponents are not quoted as making a direct objection to Cyril's position; rather, Cyril presents a conditional scenario (ἐὰν ἀνέλωμεν...) in which opponents 'will say' (ἐροῦσιν) a question that would follow from that scenario. The opponents' voice is hypothetical/future, not a quoted actual objection.
